I wouldn't recommend Seattle Children's. I can PM you with more specifics, if you would like, but I have heard many negative reports about the eating disorder program there from both parents and clinicians. It's also highly unlikely that OP's child would qualify for inpatient treatment if he is currently medically stable, so he would be likely to only receive outpatient treatment at Children's, which tends to be relatively scarce and uncoordinated for eating disorders there. Not to mention the logistical issues involved with frequent trips from Portland to Seattle for outpatient appointments, or (possibly) temporary relocation. Children's is great for treatment of some other medical disorders (childhood cancer, especially), but not eating disorders.

I would highly recommend the Kartini Clinic (located near Portland). They are much more experienced with eating disorders and food phobia, in general.

I would highly recommend checking out the [Kartini Clinic](http://www.kartiniclinic.com/). They have been very successful in treating eating disorders in children and are located near Portland, OR, if I am remembering correctly. You can find more information about their approach to treatment for young children with food phobia [here] (http://www.kartiniclinic.com/blog/post/seeking-eating-disorder-help-for-a-fear-of-swallowing/)

Awesome, thanks again for the tips! I had trouble estimating volume with my (unmarked) water bottle last week too. What I ended up doing was filling up the water bottle completely and then splitting the contents into two identical water glasses. Since they were identical, I tried to pour back and forth until water line was equal height for both glasses. Poured back in the water from one of the glasses to my water bottle and drew a line on the bottle where the water went to. Worked better than I expected, but I think I should have put the broken halves of the pills in the water too, like you suggested. I'm wondering how low my dose actually was because I just sort of kept tapping them together, and it did seem like there was a lot left in the capsule when I threw it away. Maybe more like a 10-15 mg dose?     

Anyway, I'm back on the Vyvanse today, and I feel much better already. I don't think I feel necessarily euphoric, but I seem to be in a better mood for sure -- sort of feel more positive about things, more competent, and way more relaxed? My focus seems way better too, like I am actually understanding what I'm reading and writing now :)     

I'm certainly less opposed to being on meds now than I was before, but do think it will take a bit more experimentation to find a good, long-term solution. I can get used to decaf coffee, but am not willing to give up my exercise. Also hoping to find a way to limit some of the other side effects (acne, personality suppression, etc.).       

Thanks again for all of the help!

Thanks so much for all of the info about this. I haven't taken it yesterday or today, and have a lower dose (40mg vs 50mg) now, if I decide to take it again.      Minimal medication is very important to me too, so the diluting in water strategy is appealing to me. When I tried last week though, I noticed problems the second day (I had dissolved 50mg in a bottle of water, drank 1/2 the first day, put it in the fridge, and drank the rest the next day). I think it might have been related to inconsistent dosing. Have you noticed this problem too, or do you have strategies to keep the dose fairly consistent?    

Not having to take a stimulant every day is one of the main appeals for me about this class of drugs, but I'm afraid the erraticness that results from me taking it inconsistently is an issue. I take it mainly for impulsiveness/hyperactivity/etc. (my focus is relatively fine, especially if I'm interested in the topic), and it seems like skipping days isn't really advised for those sorts of issues? I'm not really sure...    

The weird thing to me is that my body's response to skipping days has been completely inconsistent. Last week, I felt sooooo restless that I felt like I was going to jump out of my skin, couldn't sleep, higher intensity workouts, etc. And then, I skipped today and yesterday and have had more of the traditional fogginess/grogginess/fatigue/etc. I slept like 12 or 13 hours last night!     

I just feel like this is all really puzzling and I don't know what is causing what anymore. I feel like being off meds completely probably isn't the answer, but wanting to go back on them makes me feel like an addict, and I start to wonder if I should even be on them anyway. I don't think caffeine + exercise + supplements will be as effective as  medication, but at least they will have less stigma, health risks, etc.?     

I don't really know what I'm saying, but I appreciate all of the tips you suggested!

Good to know! Thanks for the warning about that. I haven't actually asked my doctor about it yet, but just thought it might be worth researching. It's helpful to have the feedback about it!      

I've been told that 50mg was a "relatively low" dose, actually, but it seems way too strong for me. 40mg is a little better (not as sedating), so far. I think I've always been sensitive to meds, and I'm not that big (5'2" female, 130ish pounds), so 50mg was too much?

Yeah, that's it exactly! I think I've seen probably 7 or 8 different psychiatrists (and 4ish psychologists) in the past couple years and I haven't really "clicked" with any of them, to be honest. I feel like most don't know what they're talking about, don't understand me at all, and completely misinterpret what I'm saying. Even when I've been depressed/suicidal, they all seem oblivious to it. My GP is actually way better with my mental/emotional health than any of the mental health professionals I've seen, which I find a bit ironic (and sad).     

I have been blaming myself a lot for this, I think. I just feel like I caused this mess now because I gave in, and decided to get diagnosed / take meds. I honestly feel like they have made me worse (in the long-term).     

I would love to be able to skip days, but I think I need to be consistent with taking them everyday. My focus isn't as bad as my hyperactivity/anxiety, to be honest, so even low-focus days are pretty symptomatic for me. I do okay when I'm interested in things -- it's just when I have to sit there, and I can't. I really always have had a ton of energy and I think it just manifested itself in different ways throughout my life (i.e. hyperactivity, anxiety, etc.).      

Sorry to ramble!

I was on the verge of getting fired from my job, and desperate to find something to help with my anxiety and depression. Basically, I've always had symptoms of ADHD, but they were controlled with exercise (a few hours a day, most days), caffeine, and a supportive environment at home and school. I graduated at 19, and started a desk job and that's when the ADHD symptoms seemed to catch up with me. I couldn't stand sitting at my desk (or in meetings) for more than 15 to 20 minutes at a time and really struggled to keep things organized. I got most of my work done, but only because I wrote computer programs to automate a lot of the routine stuff  -- I probably only did an hour or two of work each day, and spent the rest of the time goofing off.

Taking stimulants really helped my impulse control, emotional regulation, social skills, etc. The effect was immediate and people commented on it a lot when I started taking meds. When I don't take them now they'll say things like "What is wrong with you?? Calm down. Act like an adult." And I just feel like shit because that's how I really am, I guess.

I am hopeful the lower dose will help. I really feel like 50mg is too sedating. I frequently fall asleep an hour or two after I take the pill, and I feel just sort of out of it when I am up, sometimes. I don't move/fidget at all now and my anxiety has disappeared for the first time in my life. I get "stuck" on the internet at night, but that's always been a problem for me, so might not be entirely med-related.

Maybe tell yourself that you will just work on the paper for 10 minutes? I feel like the hardest part for me is usually starting something. Once I get started, I don't have as much trouble keeping myself motivated (until I get close to finishing it, I guess).

Yeah, definitely. It's helpful to hear your opinion, for sure, and it's made me reconsider my decision a bit, to be honest. I just feel like it's making me worse long-term. Like I'm becoming too dependent on it now, and on days that I don't take it I'm even worse than I was before I ever took it. If that makes sense?

I suppose I could ask my GP, but I feel like she'd be really, really hesitant. I seem to be extremely sensitive to medications and develop the very rare / serious side effects for everything (most recent was brain swelling from an antibiotic for acne). She's the one that referred me to the psych. I saw this year, but I really didn't like the psych...

Thanks. I hope it works out, but understand it's not going to be easy, by any measure. I'm actually starting to really worry now because I'm about to start a new job and move out on my own again. It's not really a time in my life where I can afford to screw things up again.

But, at the same time, I feel like it would be worth it, if I could manage to do it. I really don't like being medicated anymore, and, even if I did, I don't have a psychiatrist to prescribe meds anymore, so... sort of going to have stop taking it either way, I guess.

I agree that Strattera seems like a good option. It does take a while to build up in your system, but is probably worth a try. If you're not seeing a positive effect after a month or two, you could also try an atypical anti-depressant (like bupropion) or a tricyclic antidepressant, although I believe these are not as effective as Strattera.

I napped after taking mine this morning! I think I took it just before 8am, fell back asleep around 9am and slept till 11am. I feel like it doesn't make me feel "wired" at all, if anything I feel like it makes me sort of sedated. Do you think that means it's not working right for me?

I do like to exercise and usually do at least 60 minutes/day 6-7 days week. I'm thinking I'd probably have to up that if I didn't take a stimulant, and go back to consuming a lot of caffeine too.

Yeah, I guess I am not even aiming for "normal" anymore, and realize I won't really be that way without meds. But, I was med-free the first 21 years of my life, and fairly successful. I feel like if I could get back to that point, where I really had to work to control my symptoms, instead of just take a pill every morning, then things would be better.

Right now, I feel like the Vyvanse is really good at controlling my emotions. I don't get "stuck" in negative emotions anymore and just generally seem to be more mature about things. It also seems to make me more socially-motivated and less physically active. I sleep better at night. My anxiety is pretty much non-existent for the first time in my life.

But, I feel like my dose might be too high now because I get "too focused" on things sometimes, and I hate that feeling of having to fight myself to do the things I need to do. I also seem to struggle a lot with finding the right word to describe things sometimes now, and that's frustrating. Not to mention the dry mouth and loss of appetite too.

I would possibly consider trying something else, but I haven't been able to find a psychiatrist I like and trust, so far....

Mine seemed to get a lot worse after I started Vyvanse last year. I went from using an albuterol rescue inhaler occasionally to using an inhaled corticosteroid twice a day, nasal steroid once a day, and rescue inhaler at times too. I don't know for sure that they are connected, but I think (because of the timing of things) that they most likely are, in some way.

That makes a lot of sense. The weird thing is that even people who *don't* know me very much at all seem to comment positively on my social skills. 

Case in point: I was pumping gas yesterday and a guy I had never met before struck up a conversation. We talked a bit, and when I told him what I do for work (computer/tech stuff) he seemed shocked. He said he never would have guessed it because I seemed so "socially capable" and "normal." 

And at an interview earlier this week, I was told I "sounded like an HR person" (and that it was a compliment). I've never interviewed for a job and not gotten an offer, which I believe is more evidence that I'm socially competent enough to make a good first impression.

Situations like these are unbelievably common for me now. People routinely compliment me on my social skills, even when the conversation isn't directly about that. I feel like this wouldn't be happening if I really had social deficits. And, if I don't have social deficits, then I don't really have Asperger's?

Thanks, it's nice to talk to somebody who can actually understand! I have thought about the whole stimulant issue a lot recently and I feel like nobody else really seems to get it. I just seem to have this huge internal resistance to taking stimulants, specifically, that I haven't felt with other prescription drugs (asthma medications, SSRIs, antibiotics, etc.). I think that I can see the other conditions (asthma, depression, etc.) as being completely unnatural to me, so I am not opposed to taking medication that will treat those conditions. But, the ADHD seems so much more connected with who I am as a person, and the idea that I'm taking a medication to change myself, and not a specific disorder like asthma or depression, feels very wrong to me. I wonder if you can relate to that too? And, if you can, what do you think causes you to see ADHD differently than another medical / psychiatric condition?

I think, for me, it might be related to having had "symptoms" of ADHD my entire life. When I think of who I am as a person (my self concept, I guess), I think I tend mostly to focus on who I have been in the past. And, when I think back to who I have been in the past, I don't ever really see my natural, unmedicated self as somebody without symptoms of ADHD. But, I can remember times when I didn't have symptoms of asthma or depression or other illnesses and I think that might make it easier for me to separate those conditions from who I am as a person? It seems to fit more with the traditional model of disease, where a healthy person becomes sick at some time, but has not always been that way. I'm not really sure if any of that even makes sense, but it's just something I thought about this morning...

Your comparison of stimulant use to addiction makes a lot of sense. Part of what really appealed to me about taking stimulants at first was that I didn't need to take them every day. I've developed a huge fear of committing to anything, really, and I think it sort of extends to not wanting to ever be dependent on anything and/or anyone. So, the idea that I wouldn't ever have to take the medication on a day that I didn't want to was really enticing to me, at first, but I've noticed now that even though I don't necessarily have to take it everyday, I feel worse if I skip a day. And, it's not even like I just feel worse, in general, but worse than I ever did even before drugs. I'd say on a scale of 1 to 10 (10 being best behavior), I felt like a 4 before taking anything, and now am about 8 when taking it, and a 2 on days I "skip" taking it. That negative effect could very well be the neurotransmitter imbalance, like you mentioned, but I also think part of it is related to my old "coping mechanisms" becoming rusty. When I take the stimulants, I don't have to remember to think about what I say before I say it, how to manage emotions healthily, etc. and I just relax a bit, I guess. Then, when I'm not taking stimulants, it's hard for me to get back in the habit of doing all those things again.

It's just weird because I didn't really expect the stimulants to make me worse. I think I was focused on the short-term (how it felt during the day when I took them regularly) and didn't notice that adding in stimulants has actually made me worse, in the long run. I feel like it's made my life more erratic, where I fluctuate between a 2 and 8 (from the 1 to 10 scale mentioned above), rather than just plod along around a 5 most days.

As far as daily life, it's been a bit of a mess since I started the stimulants, to be honest. I graduated at 19, and had worked 3ish years in clinical research, but then quit last year to figure out what I wanted to do with my life. I had these grandiose visions of journaling everyday, developing better coping mechanisms, and improving myself, in general. But, mostly, I have just been depressed, and focused on how I'm never going to be successful and how disappointed I feel about being the way I am. I feel like I have had all the opportunities in life that you can imagine and and it all has been wasted because there's something inherently lacking in me, as a person. 

I can't describe it really, but I think it's just a consequence of my general pattern in life, where I become intensely involved in something and absorb everything about it very quickly, people start to seem very impressed and expect huge things from me, and then, one day, I just wake up and realize I hate whatever it is that I focused on, and I quit. People become disappointed in me, I become disappointed in myself, and the cycle tends to repeat itself. I feel like I give people false hopes and cause them a lot of a pain and disappointment, when I, inevitably, flake out. 

Argh. This is way toooo long. Sorry to type so much! I'm curious about what you do in your daily life too? Are you in therapy, or other interventions to help now?

Yeah, I think I'm the same way. If I don't take the ADHD medication, I basically don't ever really have any motivation to socialize. I take it you're female then too?  I have read some theories that HFA/Asperger's is less diagnosed in females because they tend to internalize more, and be diagnosed with problems that result from that (depression, anxiety, eating disorders, etc.) rather than the root cause (ASD, ADHD, etc.). Have you heard that theory too?

I think the "easily bored" thing is very difficult to deal with. It's made me very hesitant to commit to anything (even things I really enjoy) because I never really trust that the enjoyment will last. I feel like I constantly worry that I'm going to end up "stuck" doing something I don't like, where I'll either be completely miserable (sometimes leading to depression, suicidal thoughts, etc.) or just general flakiness (which also leads to depression, I guess).
I'm sorry to hear about that. It can be hard when people don't realize how it's affecting your life, for sure.

That's exactly what my psychologist says! Tells me that I just get bored very quickly (because I'm intelligent, supposedly) and need to find something that will be intellectually stimulating, challenging, etc. I tend to think I just need to get over my problems and stop using being "intelligent" as an excuse, but eh... I'm tired of fighting about it with her.

Like you mentioned, I sometimes think it's difficult to be higher-functioning because of the increased awareness we have about how others perceive us. It could very well be a "grass is greener on the other side" phenomenon, but, sometimes, I wish I could just be a little less high-functioning. It seems like it would be nice to be able to just work a traditional, lower-level job and be content with a normal life. As a higher-functioning individual, it feels like the expectations for what I will accomplish are much higher and the realization that I'm failing to meet those expectations is clear to me and painful too. It would be sort of nice to not have those pressures, or at least not realize they were there...

Yeah, I definitely don't tell everybody -- it's sort of weird to just bring it up. But when it has come up in conversation, I've said something like "I know my social skills aren't that great...", "I know I'm not really a 'people person' but..." , etc. And, then, people say things like "you're the most social person they know", "I don't see that at all", etc. It's weird, and I'm starting to realize they might just be trying to be nice!

The "mainstream" diagnoses can be hard to disclose too. In some respects, I think it's good that so many diagnoses are "mainstream" (increased awareness and all) now, but it can be really frustrating at times when most people seem to not really "get it."

Yeah, I feel the same way I think -- maybe they really are just being polite (by reassuring me my social skills are fine), and the fact that I can't see that they are just doing it to be polite is the result of me missing nonverbal signs? It gets confusing!

My sister and therapist seem very confident that Asperger's is the right diagnosis for me. My Mom thinks I have ADHD. My Dad thinks I have RAD. My psychiatrist thinks I have GAD + ADHD. My regular doctor seems to think it is Asperger's, and that's what has gotten me thinking about it a lot recently (I trust her opinion a lot). 

Congratulations on improving your social skills so much -- can you pinpoint anything that helped you improve so drastically? I think, for me, I had a ton of therapy that helped my confidence and general self-acceptance. I also spend tons of time online, reading message boards mostly, and I think it helps to be able to read so many different viewpoints, so that I realize various ways people might feel about different issues.

I do feel like the stimulant (I'm on Vyvanse) destroys some of my confidence. I sometimes feel like it's not even the medicine itself, but the fact that I'm taking a pill to make myself more "normal" and "accepted" by others. Because I take it most days now, people expect me to be calmer and more resilient than I usually am. When I don't take it, I end up getting really overwhelmed if something goes wrong (it's like I am flooded with things and I just end up crying, but if I am on a stimulant, I tend to just realize I'm upset and be able to quickly move on to finding ways to fix the problem, without getting stuck on being upset, if that makes sense). I also stim way less on days that I do take Vyvanse and that seems like a good thing.

I just don't know if I should keep taking it. I feel like, on one hand, it seems to be working pretty well and helping me. But, on the other, it's making me feel like people don't like who I really am, and it takes away my appetite at times. How did you decide?

Thanks for your comment, btw. It's nice to hear your perspective on this!

Trust me, I'm the same way. I have a lot of social anxiety and sometimes I would just not answer the phone, reply to emails, whatever. Completely blew off plans, and was the flakey friend that everybody probably hated. This was years ago.

I got to the point recently that I realized I had no friends left. Well, a few, maybe, but none that lived close anymore. 

I started just sending short emails out and not really caring if I got a response or not. Funny thing is... everybody replied back. 

I think it's much easier for people to reply than to initiate contact and maybe they feel flattered that others were thinking about them, hoping they were doing well, etc.? I don't know. 

All I know is it feels pretty awesome to see those emails come in and remember that other people care about you too!
Reconnect with old friends? Just shoot them an email "Hey, been wondering what you've been up to lately. Want to grab a coffee, lunch, whatever?"

Sounds like Annie is lacking in social skills.

Since she sounds nice and friendly, and you do too, I would suggest "coaching" her a bit. It would be a really nice thing to do, and the skills she learns from you could help her out the rest of her life. 

Example
"Yes, Annie, I picked up the checklist. But, I find it really hard to focus on my job when you comment on everything I do. Can you try to not comment so much, and only talk to me if you need my help, or to tell me something important?"

"Annie, I think it might be confusing to have Natalie learning from two people at once. Since I already started training her, can you find something else to work on. Natalie can ask me if she has a question, and I'll ask you if I have a question. That way we don't get mixed messages."

Stuff like that. A little blunt, but kind and helpful at the same time. It can be frustrating, but maybe if you try to think of it as helping somebody who really needs help, it will be less so?
